title: Rising from the bow
hookLine: you rise saying Allah hears whoever praises Him

lines: A SENTENCE ON THE WAY UP.
cards: A message marked read, and no reply. A joke at dinner that lands on nobody. A voicemail that may never be played.
A lot of what gets said goes out with no sign of where it lands. In the prayer, the bow is over, and the body comes back up.
On the way up, before the person is even straight, the one leading says a sentence about exactly that. Not a request. A statement.

teach.b: Rising from the bow, the one leading the prayer says: sami'a Allahu liman hamidah. Allah hears whoever praises Him. Sami'a means He heard, He hears, with the sense of listening and answering.

Then, standing straight, the people answer: rabbana wa laka al-hamd. Our Lord, and to You be the praise. Notice the shape: one voice says God hears, and everyone replies with praise, as if to say, then hear this.

The scholars call this standing position i'tidal, straightening, and like the bow, it isn't a pass-through. Yesterday's hadith, the man who prayed too fast, includes it: rise until you are standing straight.
Now the story that makes this moment well-known. It's in Bukhari, from a companion named Rifa'a ibn Rafi'.

teach.h: OUR LORD, AND TO YOU BE THE PRAISE.
teach.b: One day, praying behind the Prophet ﷺ, a man rose from the bow and, after our Lord and to You be the praise, added a few words of his own: praise, abundant, good and blessed.
When the prayer ended, the Prophet asked who had said it. The man said, I did.

teach.h: ANGELS RACING TO WRITE IT DOWN.
teach.b: And the Prophet said he had seen thirty-some angels racing each other to be the first to write it down.
One person, one sentence of praise in a line of worshippers, and in the hadith, angels hurry to record it.
In the tradition's reading, that is what sami'a Allahu liman hamidah promises: praise doesn't vanish into the room. It is heard.

how: Rising from the bow, the prayer leader says sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, and the congregation, standing straight and still, responds rabbana wa laka al-hamd before going down to prostrate.

o: a stretch you do before going to sleep
standing up to greet a guest at the door
standing still and straight after the bow

games.q: who says what on the way up — tap the pairs.
p: our Lord, and to You be the praise
told the story of the angels

s: rising from the bow is just a way to get to the ground
it's its own position, i'tidal: rise until you stand straight.
the Prophet ﷺ praised a man who added his own words of praise here
he said he saw thirty-some angels racing to write them down (Bukhari).
sami'a Allahu liman hamidah is a request
it's a statement: Allah hears whoever praises Him.

games.q: you're praying in a line behind the Prophet ﷺ. rising from the bow, you add a few words of praise no one else says. after the prayer, he asks who said them. what happens?
o: he tells you not to add anything
he says he saw angels racing to write them down
games.why: in Bukhari, the man admits it, and the Prophet says he saw thirty-some angels hurrying to be first to record it.

practice: Stand, bend forward with your hands on your knees, and hold for a breath; then come up slowly, a little at a time, until you're straight.

If you pray, whisper sami'a Allahu liman hamidah as you rise, and, standing, rabbana wa laka al-hamd. If you don't, just notice the moment of arriving upright, and stay there, straight and still, for three breaths before you sit.

wordCard.voice: I'tidal, the standing position after the bow, where the one leading says Allah hears whoever praises Him, and all answer: our Lord, and to You be the praise.

orig.note: Arabic: Allah hears whoever praises Him, said while rising from the bow.

carryVoice: Your line: he hears. In the hadith, even one added sentence had angels racing. That's one hundred four.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 799 (Rifa'a ibn Rafi': the angels racing to write the added praise)
Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (rise until you stand straight)
Sahih al-Bukhari 796 (when the imam says sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, say rabbana wa laka al-hamd)
